clue.text: By end of June, school turned out exam plan

indicators.note: a thing turned out has had its insides emptied, so only the shell of the word stays
standing by something means sitting next to it, so one piece is placed beside the other

parts.note: SCH is the standard abbreviation for school
the word emptied of its middle two letters, keeping only the outside

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the month

explanation.surface: A school's timetable for the summer exams is published at the end of June.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned out' reads as a school letting pupils go, but here it means gutted, like a pocket turned out, so only the word's outer letters survive.
explanation.definitionFit: A scheme is a systematic programme of action, a straightforward synonym for a plan or design.

clue.text: Excellent student leaving joint by front of garage

indicators.note: whatever is leaving goes away, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: a spliff is a cannabis cigarette, slang for a joint
L for learner, the usual crossword student, which is removed
'by' and 'in' both mean during, as in 'by night' or 'in the night'

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A star pupil skips out of the pub to smoke a joint next to the garage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' does double duty in crosswords: here it means during, as in 'by day'. Spiffing is a jolly, old-fashioned British word of approval.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiffing is dated British slang meaning splendid or first-rate, a direct equivalent of excellent.

clue.text: Half a month in poor group that can't agree

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: poor in the sense of going without food

indicators.note: half a word keeps just one of its halves, here the opening pair of letters

parts.note: the first half of JUNE or JULY, which both begin the same way

explanation.surface: For two weeks of the month a hard-up committee can't reach a decision.
explanation.walkthrough: June and July begin with the same two letters, so it does not matter which month is meant. 'Poor' here means short of food rather than money.
explanation.definitionFit: A hung jury is a panel of jurors unable to reach a verdict, so it is literally a body that fails to agree.

clue.text: Before 4, came up to Lorraine's place?

indicators.note: one thing coming before another fixes the order in which the parts are joined

parts.note: to come up to expectations is to have met them
the answer at 4 is VARIABLE, and Z is a typical algebraic variable

explanation.surface: Someone approached a woman called Lorraine's house just before four o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: '4' is not a time but a cross-reference to 4 Across, VARIABLE; Z is a variable, as in x, y and z. The question mark flags Lorraine as a region, not a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Metz is a city in the Lorraine region of north-eastern France, so it is one place in Lorraine.

clue.text: Unsteady adult, breaking bone, grabbed by curt manservant

indicators.note: something breaking into a thing gets inside it, splitting it
curt means cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a valet is a gentleman's personal manservant; trimmed to VALE

indicators.note: whatever is grabbed is held inside the grip of something else

parts.note: the rib is a bone of the chest
A is the film certificate abbreviation for adult

explanation.surface: A drunken grown-up breaks a bone and has to be held up by the abrupt butler.
explanation.walkthrough: Two containers nest here: the adult goes into the bone first, and that pair then goes into the clipped servant.
explanation.definitionFit: Variable means liable to change or fluctuate, which is close in sense to unsteady or inconstant.

clue.text: Number one local bond seen under contents of bank statement

indicators.note: in a down clue, being under something means being placed after it
the contents of a word are its inner letters, without the ends

parts.note: the inside letters of the word
NO is the standard abbreviation for number
'un is a dialect form of one, as in 'a good 'un'
cement binds things together, so it is a bond

explanation.surface: A town's leading building society bond is listed below the details on a bank statement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' marks a regional form of 'one'. NO + UN + CEMENT, a single chain, goes under AN, because it is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An announcement is a formal public declaration, which makes it one kind of statement.

clue.text: ITV News regularly shows US composer

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: A British television bulletin features an American composer.
explanation.walkthrough: ITV is a British commercial television channel. Ignore the space and take every other letter from the start.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Ives was a modernist American composer, known for works such as The Unanswered Question.

clue.text: Extra legal action, principally with inferred regulation

parts.note: in cricket a bye is a run scored as an extra, not off the bat

indicators.note: principal means chief or first, so each word gives its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letters of the two words
W is the standard abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: A lawyer stretches a rule by claiming an extra legal step is implied by it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extra' is a cricket term: a bye is a run given away when the ball passes the batter and wicketkeeper untouched.
explanation.definitionFit: A bye-law is a rule made by a local authority or company, a particular sort of regulation.

clue.text: Office workers finally qualified, standing for respect

indicators.note: finally points at the end of each word, so the closing letters are kept

parts.note: the closing letter of each word

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing up means reading from the bottom upwards

parts.note: meet as an old adjective means suitable or fit, as in 'it is meet that'

explanation.surface: Clerks who have finally passed their exams gain standing and respect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Qualified' is not passing exams; it is the archaic adjective MEET, meaning fit, which is then turned upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Esteem as a noun is high regard or admiration, a near synonym of respect.

clue.text: Fire string of marketing interns following setback

indicators.note: a setback sends things backwards, so the letters are read in the opposite direction
a string is a run of consecutive letters, so the word is a stretch of the text

parts.note: the letters spanning the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: After a business downturn, a company sacks its marketing interns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire' looks like the sacking in the surface but it is the definition, meaning to set alight.
explanation.definitionFit: To fire something is to set it burning, which is exactly what to ignite means.

clue.text: Street criminal pursues home advantage

indicators.note: what pursues comes after, so this piece goes second

parts.note: being in means being at home

indicators.note: something criminal is bent or crooked, so the letters are bent out of order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A mugger chases someone home, sensing an opportunity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Street criminal' reads as one thing, a mugger, but 'criminal' is the signal acting on 'Street'.
explanation.definitionFit: Interest can mean benefit or advantage, as in acting in someone's best interest.

clue.text: Revolutionary new beers suppressing desire for fast food

parts.note: Che Guevara is the crossword's favourite revolutionary

indicators.note: to suppress is to hold down and keep in, so one part is held within the other
something new is made afresh, so these letters are remade in a different order

parts.note: the letters to be reordered
an urge is a strong desire

explanation.surface: A radical's fresh brews dampen any appetite for junk food.
explanation.walkthrough: Che Guevara is the standard crossword revolutionary. The rearranged drinks wrap round the desire, which lands just before their last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheeseburger is a hamburger topped with cheese, a staple item of fast food.

clue.text: Peak form uplifted job interview from the start

indicators.note: the start of each word is its first letter, so only those are kept

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A candidate in top shape feels buoyed by how the job interview went.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peak form' looks like one phrase, but 'Peak' stands alone as the definition and 'form' starts the run of initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Fuji is Japan's highest mountain, a volcanic peak southwest of Tokyo.

clue.text: Pick up footwear for pets

indicators.note: to pick up a sound is to hear it, so the answer is what is heard

parts.note: items of footwear, said out loud

explanation.surface: Someone collects little boots and shoes for their dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pets' is the French sense: 'mon chou', literally 'my cabbage', is a French term of endearment, and choux is its plural, pronounced like shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: In French, chou is an affectionate name for a darling, so choux are dear ones or pets.

clue.text: Scold class

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an old verb for telling someone off angrily
second meaning: a grade or rank

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it suggests a teacher scolding a class; the two words are separate meanings of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: To rate someone is to berate them, and a rate is a grade or ranking, as in second-rate.

clue.text: Stephen maybe insulates old flooring

indicators.note: insulating wraps something round, so one part is surrounded by the other

parts.note: Stephen was an English king, and Stephen King is a novelist
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Perhaps a builder called Stephen lays insulation under an old floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flooring' is not floorboards but the verb: knocking someone down. A KO is a knockout in boxing.
explanation.definitionFit: KOing someone means knocking them out, putting them on the canvas, which is to floor them.

clue.text: School in south-east China

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: SE is the compass abbreviation
a pod is a group of whales or dolphins, as a school is

explanation.surface: A school is located in the south-east of China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' is not the country but porcelain; the capital letter is just its place at the start of the phrase. School and pod both mean a group of sea mammals.
explanation.definitionFit: Spode is a famous make of English porcelain from Stoke-on-Trent, so it is a type of china.

clue.text: Squeak made by pointy object cutting new key

indicators.note: a thing cutting into another goes inside it and splits it

parts.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
Escape is a key on a computer keyboard
an arrow is a sharp-tipped missile

explanation.surface: A sharp tool makes a squeaky noise as it cuts a fresh key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squeak' is not the sound; it is the noun in 'a close squeak' or 'a narrow squeak'. The key is on a keyboard, not a keyring.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow squeak is British slang for a close shave, the same idea as a narrow escape.

clue.text: At first just mimics absorbing a north European language

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

indicators.note: to absorb is to take in, so one part ends up inside the other

parts.note: to ape someone is to imitate them
A taken as written, and N for north
E is the standard abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A beginner copies phrases to soak up a Scandinavian tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface steers towards a Nordic language, but 'north European' is split up for letters; the definition is just 'language'.
explanation.definitionFit: Japanese is the language spoken in Japan, so it is one example of a language.

clue.text: Compulsory mass, shortly burying king that's died

indicators.note: to bury something is to hide it inside, so one part goes within another
made short, the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a requiem is a mass for the dead; trimmed to REQUIE
R for rex, Latin for king
D is the abbreviation for died, as in family trees

explanation.surface: Attendance at a funeral mass for a dead monarch is obligatory.
explanation.walkthrough: The shortened REQUIEM holds R before its last letter, and D follows the whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Something required is demanded by rule, which is what compulsory or obligatory means.

clue.text: Go-between retained item under the table

indicators.note: someone under the table is too drunk to stand, and drunk letters are all over the place

parts.note: all twelve letters of the two words, to be reordered

explanation.surface: A middleman keeps back a little something as a backhander.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under the table' suggests a secret bribe, but it means drunk, the signal to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun an intermediate is a mediator who acts between two parties, just like a go-between.

clue.text: Departure of base topless man-eater

indicators.note: without a top, the word loses its opening letter, which in a down clue sits at the top

parts.note: e is the base of natural logarithms in mathematics
an ogress is a female ogre, a giant that eats people

explanation.surface: A scantily clad femme fatale walks out of a military base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man-eater' suggests a predatory woman, but here it is literal: a female ogre. The 'base' is the mathematical constant e.
explanation.definitionFit: Egress is the act of going out or leaving a place, a formal word for a departure.

clue.text: Female boxer once linked to foreign agents

indicators.note: linking joins two things end to end, so one part follows the other

parts.note: Muhammad Ali, the former world heavyweight boxing champion
the CIA is the American intelligence agency, foreign from a British view

explanation.surface: A former women's boxing champion turns out to have ties to spies overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Female boxer' reads as one person, but the definition is 'Female' alone: a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Alicia is a girl's name, so it can stand for a female as setters use the word in names.

clue.text: Au naturel, at last appearing in Apollo, say

indicators.note: something appearing in another shows up inside it

parts.note: Apollo is a Greek god, given as one example

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter, which is the only one kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A naked figure finally shows up as a statue of Apollo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Au naturel' means nude and seems to describe the statue, but 'Au' is the definition: the chemical symbol for gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Au, from the Latin aurum, is the chemical symbol for the element gold.

clue.text: Financial statistician's issue, one of four brief books

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the word drops its final letter

parts.note: issue means offspring, and a quad is one of quadruplets
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A finance analyst's problem is having only four short books to consult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' is children, not a problem: one of four children born together is a quad, cut to QUA.
explanation.definitionFit: Quant is City slang for a quantitative analyst, who applies mathematics and statistics to markets.

clue.text: Something fired by 18 from back-to-back antagonists in Falklands War

indicators.note: two things standing back to back each face away, so each is turned round

parts.note: AR is the code for Argentina, one side in the 1982 war
the United Kingdom, the other side in the conflict

explanation.surface: Someone describes a weapon fired in the Falklands War of 1982.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fired' suggests a gun, but it means baked in a kiln; 18 is JAPANESE, so the answer is Japanese pottery.
explanation.definitionFit: Raku is a Japanese ware fired at low temperature and pulled from the kiln hot, used in tea ceremonies.

clue.text: Charge loadsa money for installing opening in roof

indicators.note: installing something puts it inside, so one part goes within another

parts.note: a wad is a thick bundle of banknotes

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A builder demands a fortune for putting a skylight in the roof.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loadsamoney' was a brash, cash-waving comic character of 1980s Britain; here it just means a wad of cash.
explanation.definitionFit: A ward is a person, often a child, placed in someone's care, that is, in their charge.

clue.text: Progressively dance yourself dizzy, deserving forty winks

indicators.note: progressively means step by step, so each word gives a letter one place further in

parts.note: the first letter
the second letter
the third letter
the fourth letter

explanation.surface: After dancing till your head spins, you've earned a short nap.
explanation.walkthrough: First letter of the first word, second of the next, and so on through four words.
explanation.definitionFit: Forty winks is an idiom for a short light sleep, which is a doze or nap.

clue.text: Swap farthings and sixpences, perhaps

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a trade of one thing for another
second meaning: coins no longer in use, so former loose coins, read as two parts

explanation.walkthrough: Farthings (quarter pennies) and sixpences are old British coins withdrawn when currency went decimal in 1971, so they are EX (former) CHANGE.
explanation.definitionFit: An exchange is a trade in which one thing is given for another, the same as a swap.

clue.text: One affected by tough question about university

indicators.note: about means around, so one part surrounds another

parts.note: a poser is a puzzling problem
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A student is thrown by a hard question about their university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affected' reads as upset, but 'One affected' means a person who puts on airs.
explanation.definitionFit: A poseur is a pretentious person who behaves in an artificial way to impress, an affected individual.

clue.text: Norm's position — heading firm for the Krays?

indicators.note: heading off means losing the head, so the word drops its first letter

parts.note: a stand is a position or stance taken
firm means hard, said as East End Londoners would, dropping the H

explanation.surface: A man called Norm takes charge of a gang like the Krays.
explanation.walkthrough: The Krays were twin gangsters from London's East End, where Cockney speech drops the H, so 'hard' becomes 'ard. 'Firm' also hints at their gang.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is an accepted level or benchmark that things are measured against, which is a norm.

clue.text: Saw puppy, barely sleeping?

parts.note: a sleeper is in bed

indicators.note: bare means stripped, so the outside letters are taken off and only the inside kept

parts.note: a whelp is a puppy; its inner letters are kept

explanation.surface: Someone spotted a young dog that was scarcely asleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' could be the tool, but it is the past tense of see. A whelp is a puppy; 'barely' strips its ends, and the question mark flags 'sleeping' as a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Beheld is the past tense of behold, an old word meaning looked at or saw.
